title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Runbooks, and Incident Review
author: Ari Chen
body:
Overview

This page codifies Redwood Inference's SRE standards for defining and operating Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning and forecasting, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling expectations, and runbook conventions. The goal is consistent, measurable service reliability across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments while enabling product velocity.

Scope

Applies to: all customer-facing inference services, API gateway, model-routing services, and critical platform components (autoscaler, KV cache, datastore). Not intended for short-lived feature prototypes — use product-team doc for those.

Principles

- Measurable: SLOs must be expressible as precise metrics and computed from production telemetry.
- Actionable: Error budget policies must enable engineering tradeoffs (rollouts, throttling, mitigation).
- Owned: Every SLO has a defined owner and on-call responsible for response and remediation.
- Predictable: Capacity planning should aim to keep 95th percentile latency within SLO under expected peaks.
- Learn & Improve: Post-incident reviews must identify root cause and an owner for follow-up reliability initiatives.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Purpose

SLOs express customer-facing reliability expectations and guide prioritization of reliability work. Error budgets quantify acceptable deviation and support tolerating failures while enabling safe releases.

Definitions

- Availability SLO: Percentage of successful requests over a rolling evaluation window (typically 30d).
- Latency SLO: Percentage of requests under a threshold (e.g., p95 < 250ms) over the evaluation window.
- Error Budget: 1 - SLO (for availability) or allowable percentage of failing requests.
- Burn Rate: Rate at which the error budget is consumed.

Required fields for any SLO document

- SLO name and short description
- Metric source (prometheus metric, tracing span, synthetic check) with query
- Evaluation window (e.g., 7d, 30d)
- Target (e.g., 99.95%)
- Owner (team + on-call alias)
- Alerting thresholds (warning, critical)
- Error budget policy (actions on burn thresholds)

Example SLO table

| Service | SLO type | Metric (prometheus) | Window | Target | Owner | Critical action |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| inference-api (text-gen) | Availability | sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=\"inference-api\",code!~\"5..\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=\"inference-api\"}[5m])) | 30d | 99.95% | inference-team / oncall@redwood.example.com | Rollback canary, throttle non-essential traffic |
| inference-api (p95) | Latency | histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"inference-api\"}[5m])) by (le)) | 7d | p95 < 250ms | inference-team | Reduce batch sizes, increase pool size |

Error budget policies (standard)

1. Burn < 1.0x: Normal operations.
2. Burn >= 1.0x and < 3.0x for 1h: Pause low-risk rollouts; prioritize mitigations.
3. Burn >= 3.0x for 1h or any critical alert: Initiate emergency response; consider automated rollback or capacity bump.
4. If error budget exhausted for evaluation window: Stop all non-critical changes, open reliability initiative ticket with RCA and remediation plan.

Procedures (SLO lifecycle)

1. Define SLO in an SLO doc (see required fields).
2. Review quarterly (owner responsible) and update thresholds or metrics.
3. If missing instrumentation, create observability ticket and schedule within next sprint.
4. If SLO violated, follow incident review process and generate reliability initiative.

2) Capacity Planning

Goals

- Ensure the platform has headroom to meet SLOs during expected bursts.
- Provide transparent forecasts to finance and sales for Dedicated/reserved capacity.

Inputs

- Historical telemetry (7d/30d/90d) for request rate, token rate, sequence length distribution.
- Business forecasts (expected new customers, promotions).
- Model changes (new models often change compute profile).
- Planned releases and rolling maintenance windows.

Process (quarterly planning + rolling 30d)

1. Forecast demand: teams provide expected growth; SRE projects infrastructure need using workload-characterization scripts.
2. Compute required GPU-hours with baseline unit economics and tail-latency targets.
3. Identify capacity gaps and mitigation options (autoscale policy, model quantization, batching changes, regional spillover).
4. Approve budget and schedule procurement or cloud reservations if month-to-month gap > 15% of committed capacity.

Sizing checklist

- p50/p95/p99 latency targets under expected peak load
- CPU/GPU utilization targets (steady-state GPU util target: 60–80% for Dedicated pools)
- Cold-start counts and amortized startup time for private deployments
- Batching loss vs latency tradeoffs documented

Capacity runbooks (excerpt)

- Quickscale (manual): increase pool size via infra-ops UI and notify traffic router to rebalance.
- Emergency: enable burst pool (pre-warmed instances) and temporarily lower model quality (quantized variant) for non-critical routes.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Prioritization

- Every SRE quarter includes a reliability roadmap that maps top error budget risks to initiatives (e.g., KV cache hardening, autoscaler tuning, network egress optimization).
- Prioritization criteria: SLO impact, customer impact, effort estimate, cross-team dependency.
- Initiative format: concise description, metrics to improve, owner, milestone dates, and rollback criteria.

4) Incident Review Standards (Postmortems)

Required timeline

- Declare incident severity within 15 minutes of first critical alert.
- Incident commander assigned within 30 minutes.
- Initial incident brief to stakeholders within 2 hours.
- Postmortem draft within 3 business days; finalized with action owners within 10 business days.

Postmortem template (required fields)

- Title
- Incident ID and timeline (timestamps, detection, mitigation, resolution)
- Impact summary (customers affected, SLOs impacted, duration)
- Root cause analysis (technical cause and contributing factors)
- Actions taken (immediate mitigations, temporary workarounds)
- Corrective actions (long-term fixes) with owners and due dates
- Lessons learned and follow-ups

Blamelessness policy

- Focus on systemic causes and process improvements. Individual errors are not the main deliverable. If personnel issues emerge, handle via private HR or engineering management channels.

5) Operational Tooling and Observability Expectations

Dashboards and metrics

- Each SLO must have a public dashboard with: SLO rolling calculation, burn rate, alert log, and top contributing error classes.
- Standard dashboards include: API health, model-inference pipeline, autoscaler view, GPU utilization, queue lengths, and frontend latency distribution.

Alerting rules

- Alerts must be meaningful with actionable runbook links. Avoid noisy alerts; use multi-window rules (5m and 1h windows) to reduce flapping.
- Severity mapping: P1 (page on-call), P2 (notify in channel), P3 (ticket for next sprint).

Tracing and logs

- Distributed traces must include request ID and model-id tags.
- Structured logs with standardized keys: service, request_id, route, model_version, latency_ms, error_code.

Tooling standards

- Prometheus for metrics ingestion; Grafana for dashboards; Tempo/Jaeger for tracing; Loki/Elasticsearch for logs.
- Use alertmanager for deduplication and routing.
- Synthetic checks: production canary queries from at least 3 regions every 1 minute.

6) Runbook Standards and Templates

Runbook requirements

- One runbook per critical alert class. Runbooks must include: symptom, likely causes (top 3), immediate steps to mitigate, commands/URLs for mitigation, owner, escalation path, and verification steps.
- Keep runbooks short and actionable (< 1 page preferred).

Runbook snippet (example)

Title: inference-api-high-p95
Symptom: p95 latency > 300ms for > 5 minutes
Likely causes:
- Batching increased beyond configured max
- GPU saturation on pool A
- Downstream datastore slowdown
Immediate mitigation steps:
1. Check dashboard: https://grafana/redwood/inference-api
2. If GPU util > 95% on primary pool: scale up pool A (infra-ops -> pool -> +2 nodes)
3. If queue length > 1000: enable request-throttling for non-critical routes: curl -X POST https://router/api/throttle -d '{"routes":["/embeddings"]}'
4. If datastore errors present: route traffic to read-replica (traffic-router -> reroute)
Verification: p95 drops under 250ms for 15 minutes and error budget burn rate returns < 1.0x

Formatting and storage

- Runbooks stored in confluence under eng-sre/runbooks and mirrored as executable runbook snippets in the runbook-repo (git) for automation.

7) On-call and Ownership

- Primary on-call: first responder for incidents and actioning runbooks.
- Secondary on-call: backup for escalation and cross-team coordination.
- SLO owner: responsible for SLO definition, review cadence, and remediation when error budgets are depleted.

8) Rollout and Canary Guidance (reliability-minded deployments)

- Canary releases limited to <=5% of traffic for first 30 minutes; monitor SLO and burn rate.
- If burn rate > 2.0x during canary, automatically halt rollout and rollback to previous model variant.
- For model swaps with unknown compute profile, run performance canaries in a dedicated staging cluster with representative traffic.

Appendix: Example Prometheus queries and alert rules

SLO availability (30d):

```
ratio(sum(increase(http_requests_total{job=\"inference-api\",code!~\"5..\"}[30d])), sum(increase(http_requests_total{job=\"inference-api\"}[30d])))
```
Burn rate (1h over 30d window):

```
(1 - ratio(sum(increase(http_requests_total{job=\"inference-api\",code!~\"5..\"}[1h])), sum(increase(http_requests_total{job=\"inference-api\"}[1h])))) / (1 - 0.9995)
```
Alert rule (example):

```
- alert: InferenceAPIHighErrorBudgetBurn
  expr: burn_rate_1h > 2
  for: 15m
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    runbook: https://confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/inference-api-high-errorburn
```
